explanation: Nigeria faces both traditional undernutrition issues and a growing prevalence of lifestyle-related chronic illnesses. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T002#GNS227_U4_T002_h6)

question: Why must Nigerian dietitians adapt international guidelines to local foods?

options.A: To prevent patients from eating imported protein sources
options.B: To comply with federal laws banning foreign agricultural goods
options.C: To reduce the total number of hospital admissions for malaria
options.D: To ensure recommendations use affordable and culturally accepted items

explanation: Patients are more likely to follow dietary advice when it incorporates familiar, accessible local staples like yam and cassava. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T002#GNS227_U4_T002_h6)

question: Which healthcare worker is often first to notice daily meal intake issues on the ward?

options.A: The nurse
options.B: The radiographer
options.C: The pharmacist
options.D: The hospital accountant

explanation: Nurses spend the most time at the bedside, observing whether a patient is eating their served meals. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T002#GNS227_U4_T002_h7)

question: What is the main benefit of interprofessional collaboration in dietetics?

options.A: Reducing the working hours of medical doctors
options.B: Eliminating the need for nursing care plans
options.C: Allowing dietitians to prescribe pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: Preventing conflicting instructions and improving safety

explanation: Teamwork ensures all healthcare professionals work toward the same therapeutic goals without giving contradictory advice. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T002#GNS227_U4_T002_h7)

question: What is the primary definition of nutrients in human nutrition?

options.A: Chemical substances obtained from food needed for body function
options.B: Waste products eliminated through normal digestion
options.C: Medical compounds designed to cure chronic illnesses
options.D: Artificial supplements used to boost daily energy levels

explanation: Nutrients are the specific chemical components derived from diet that support basic physiological processes. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h1)

question: Why is dietetics important in clinical nursing practice?

options.A: It replaces the need for pharmacological interventions entirely
options.B: It calculates exact medication dosages based on weight
options.C: It guides patients in planning food choices for optimal health
options.D: It focuses solely on hospital kitchen meal preparation

explanation: Dietetics applies nutritional science to help individuals make healthy eating decisions during recovery and prevention. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h1)

question: Which macronutrient serves as the primary and most immediate source of energy for the body?

options.A: Proteins
options.B: Fats
options.C: Vitamins
options.D: Carbohydrates

explanation: Carbohydrates break down rapidly into glucose, which cells use immediately to generate energy. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h2)

question: What is the main function of dietary proteins in the body?

options.A: Simple sugars utilized for quick cellular respiration
options.B: Amino acids used for tissue repair and enzyme production
options.C: Inorganic elements required for bone mineralization
options.D: Fatty acids stored in adipose tissue for insulation

explanation: Proteins are made of amino acids that build and repair body tissues while supporting vital metabolic enzymes. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h2)

question: What distinguishes micronutrients from macronutrients?

options.A: They provide the bulk of daily caloric energy requirements
options.B: They can only be manufactured synthetically in laboratories
options.C: They are required in much smaller quantities by the body
options.D: They do not play any role in maintaining human health

explanation: Micronutrients are needed in trace amounts compared to macronutrients, yet they remain vital for regulating bodily functions. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h3)

question: Which category of micronutrients includes iron and zinc?

options.A: Water-soluble vitamins
options.B: Trace minerals
options.C: Fat-soluble vitamins
options.D: Macrominerals

explanation: Minerals needed in minute quantities, such as iron and zinc, are classified as trace minerals. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h3)

question: What is the primary function of water as a nutrient in the human body?

options.A: Regulating blood sugar levels through hormonal control
options.B: Providing the main source of daily dietary caloric energy
options.C: Acting as a solvent and transporting nutrients and wastes
options.D: Building strong skeletal structures and bone density

explanation: Water dissolves substances and serves as the primary medium for transporting nutrients and removing waste. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h4)

question: What is one of the earliest complications a patient with severe dehydration is likely to experience?

options.A: Immediate accumulation of excess adipose tissue
options.B: Rapid increase in bone mineral density
options.C: Complete cessation of red blood cell production
options.D: Impaired renal function and reduced cognitive performance

explanation: Low fluid volume quickly stresses the kidneys and affects brain function because cells lack adequate hydration. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h4)

question: Why are human digestive enzymes unable to break down dietary fiber?

options.A: Fiber lacks chemical bonds that human enzymes can digest
options.B: Bile salts neutralize fiber molecules in the duodenum
options.C: Stomach acid destroys fiber before it reaches the intestines
options.D: Pancreatic secretions convert fiber directly into gas

explanation: The human digestive tract lacks the specific enzymes needed to break the chemical bonds found in plant fiber. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h5)

question: What is the primary benefit of insoluble fiber in the digestive tract?

options.A: It dissolves completely to lower systemic blood pressure
options.B: It adds stool bulk and speeds up intestinal transit time
options.C: It binds directly to circulating dietary fats in the stomach
options.D: It provides direct cellular energy for colon lining cells

explanation: Insoluble fiber passes through largely intact, adding bulk and promoting regular bowel movements. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h5)

question: Which local food item is a primary source of complex carbohydrates in Nigerian diets?

options.A: Palm oil
options.B: Yam
options.C: Egusi
options.D: Beef

explanation: Yam is a staple root crop rich in complex carbohydrates widely consumed across Nigeria. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h6)

question: What nutritional value do local green leafy vegetables like ugu provide to patients?

options.A: Concentrated calories and simple sugars
options.B: Vitamins, iron, and dietary fiber
options.C: Essential fatty acids and cholesterol
options.D: Water-soluble animal proteins

explanation: Local greens are packed with micronutrients such as iron and vitamins, along with beneficial fiber. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h6)

question: Which assessment method measures physical dimensions like height, weight, and arm circumference?

options.A: Clinical physical examinations
options.B: Biochemical laboratory tests
options.C: Anthropometric measurements
options.D: Dietary recall interviews

explanation: Anthropometry involves physical body measurements used to evaluate growth and nutritional status. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h7)

question: What is a common clinical sign of iron deficiency anemia during a physical examination?

options.A: Yellowed sclera of eyes
options.B: Swollen lower extremities
options.C: Enlarged thyroid gland
options.D: Pale conjunctiva

explanation: Low hemoglobin levels caused by iron deficiency often result in noticeable pallor in the mucous membranes like the conjunctiva. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h7)

question: Who do nurses primarily collaborate with to create customized therapeutic meal plans for patients?

options.A: Laboratory scientists
options.B: Dietitians
options.C: Physiotherapists
options.D: Pharmacists

explanation: Dietitians are specialists trained to design medical nutrition therapy tailored to complex clinical conditions. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h8)

question: Why must nurses consider cultural food preferences when giving dietary education?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any laboratory investigations
options.B: It improves patient cooperation with recommended meal plans
options.C: It speeds up the chemical digestion of macronutrients
options.D: It reduces the financial cost of hospital food services

explanation: Patients are far more likely to follow dietary advice when it incorporates familiar and culturally accepted foods. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T003#GNS227_U4_T003_h8)

question: What does nutrient quality primarily measure in a food item?

options.A: The total number of calories per serving
options.B: The biological usefulness of the nutrients provided
options.C: The shelf life and expiration timeline
options.D: The financial cost of the food item

explanation: Nutrient quality focuses on how well the body can utilize the essential components found in food, rather than just the caloric count. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h1)

question: Why is nutrient density more important than mere caloric density for a patient?

options.A: It supplies vital vitamins and minerals without excess empty calories
options.B: It guarantees immediate weight gain and muscle development
options.C: It lowers the financial cost of hospital meals significantly
options.D: It eliminates the need for any water consumption

explanation: Nutrient-dense foods deliver high amounts of essential elements per calorie, preventing deficiencies without overloading the patient with empty energy sources. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h1)

question: What defines a complete protein source?

options.A: Being derived exclusively from plant sources
options.B: Having zero fat content and high fiber
options.C: Requiring no digestion before absorption
options.D: Containing all nine essential amino acids

explanation: Complete proteins supply all the essential amino acids that the human body cannot synthesize on its own. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h2)

question: A patient with type 2 diabetes needs advice on carbohydrate quality. What should the nurse recommend?

options.A: Refined sugars for a quick burst of energy
options.B: Saturated fats to slow down carbohydrate digestion
options.C: High-fiber complex carbohydrates to stabilize blood glucose
options.D: Low-protein starches to prevent kidney strain

explanation: Complex carbohydrates containing dietary fiber slow digestion and prevent the rapid blood glucose spikes seen with refined sugars. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h2)

question: What does micronutrient bioavailability measure?

options.A: The speed at which food passes through the stomach
options.B: The expiration date of vitamin supplements
options.C: The proportion of a nutrient absorbed and used by the body
options.D: The total weight of vitamins present in a raw food item

explanation: Bioavailability looks past ingestion to measure actual absorption and usability at the cellular level. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h3)

question: Which dietary factor enhances the absorption of non-heme iron from plant sources?

options.A: Calcium supplements
options.B: Vitamin C
options.C: Phytic acid
options.D: Dietary fiber

explanation: Ascorbic acid or vitamin C changes the chemical state of non-heme iron in the gut, making it much easier for the intestines to absorb. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h3)

question: Which group of nutrients is most easily lost during prolonged boiling in water?

options.A: Water-soluble vitamins
options.B: Insoluble minerals
options.C: Saturated fatty acids
options.D: Complex proteins

explanation: Vitamins like C and the B-vitamins dissolve into cooking water and can be lost if the liquid is discarded. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h4)

question: Why does prolonged exposure to light and oxygen reduce the quality of certain nutrients?

options.A: It hardens the mineral structure making it indigestible
options.B: It increases the total carbohydrate count of the food
options.C: It causes the chemical breakdown of sensitive vitamins
options.D: It transforms unsaturated fats into complete proteins

explanation: Environmental factors like light and oxygen trigger oxidation and degradation of delicate vitamin structures. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h4)

question: A lack of dietary vitamin C over a prolonged period leads to which clinical condition?

options.A: Rickets
options.B: Beriberi
options.C: Scurvy
options.D: Pellagra

explanation: Scurvy is the classic deficiency disease resulting from inadequate vitamin C intake, characterized by poor wound healing and connective tissue weakness. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h5)

question: Why can a patient with normal or high body weight still suffer from malnutrition?

options.A: Their body automatically destroys all ingested vitamins
options.B: Their diet may lack essential micronutrients and high-quality macronutrients
options.C: Fat cells store all necessary minerals permanently
options.D: High caloric intake neutralizes the need for proteins

explanation: Malnutrition encompasses poor nutrient quality, meaning a person can consume excess calories while remaining severely deficient in vital nutrients. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h5)

question: What is the primary focus of standard dietary guidelines for optimizing health?

options.A: Maximizing daily intake of artificial vitamin supplements
options.B: Choosing nutrient-dense whole foods over processed items
options.C: Reducing total fluid intake to prevent electrolyte imbalances
options.D: Eliminating all forms of dietary fat from the menu

explanation: Dietary guidelines consistently promote whole, nutrient-dense foods to supply adequate vitamins, minerals, and high-quality macronutrients. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h6)

question: When teaching a patient about healthy dietary patterns, what should the nurse emphasize?

options.A: Including a colorful variety of fruits and vegetables
options.B: Consuming foods with high sodium to retain water
options.C: Relying entirely on fortified meal replacement shakes
options.D: Avoiding all starchy carbohydrates completely

explanation: A diverse array of colorful produce ensures a wide spectrum of essential micronutrients and antioxidants. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T004#GNS227_U4_T004_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of nutrient quantification in clinical practice?

options.A: Calculating food costs
options.B: Determining cooking times
options.C: Increasing meal frequency
options.D: Evaluating dietary adequacy

explanation: Nutrient quantification provides objective data to determine if a patient consumes enough essential substances for health. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h1)

question: Why do nurses measure nutrients in different units like grams, milligrams, or micrograms?

options.A: Hospital policy mandates metric conversions for every meal
options.B: Patients prefer numerical values over food groups
options.C: Different nutrients are needed in vastly different amounts for safety
options.D: Laboratory equipment only reads in microgram increments

explanation: Macronutrients like proteins are measured in grams, while micronutrients like vitamins require much smaller units to prevent toxicity. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h1)

question: Which nutrient category is required by the body in large quantities measured in grams?

options.A: Macronutrients
options.B: Micronutrients
options.C: Catalytic enzymes
options.D: Trace elements

explanation: Carbohydrates, proteins, and fats make up the macronutrient group, which provides bulk energy and building blocks. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h2)

question: A patient needs elements required only in milligram amounts for metabolic regulation. Which group is this?

options.A: Micronutrients
options.B: Macronutrients
options.C: Dense lipids
options.D: Caloric polymers

explanation: Vitamins and minerals fall under micronutrients, functioning in small doses to regulate vital chemical reactions. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h2)

question: What does the acronym RDA stand for in nutritional standards?

options.A: Reference Dietary Availability
options.B: Required Daily Assessment
options.C: Recommended Dietary Allowance
options.D: Rapid Diet Adaptation

explanation: RDA represents the daily intake level estimated to meet the nutrient needs of nearly all healthy individuals. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)?

options.A: Preventing nutrient toxicity from excessive intake
options.B: Establishing the minimum daily energy requirement
options.C: Calculating basic caloric needs during illness
options.D: Determining the cheapest food sources

explanation: The UL sets the highest average daily nutrient intake level that is likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h3)

question: Which physiological state typically demands a higher intake of iron and folate?

options.A: Adult aging
options.B: Acute fasting
options.C: Pregnancy
options.D: Sedentary rest

explanation: Gestational demands require increased iron and folate to support expanded blood volume and fetal tissue growth. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h4)

question: How does chronic infection affect a patient's nutrient needs?

options.A: It stabilizes daily macronutrient utilization
options.B: It increases metabolic stress and raises nutrient needs
options.C: It neutralizes the need for all micronutrients
options.D: It decreases total energy expenditure and lowers requirements

explanation: Infection and illness elevate metabolic demands, requiring higher quantities of nutrients to support the immune response and tissue repair. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h4)

question: What is a 24-hour dietary recall?

options.A: A laboratory test measuring blood glucose levels over a day
options.B: A continuous recording of meals for an entire month
options.C: A listing of all food and beverages consumed over the past day
options.D: A strict fasting protocol prescribed before surgery

explanation: The 24-hour recall is a quick assessment method where the patient remembers and reports everything they ate or drank during the previous 24 hours. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h5)

question: A nurse asks a patient to write down food items immediately as they are eaten to avoid memory errors. Which tool is this?

options.A: Anthropometric screening
options.B: Food frequency questionnaire
options.C: 24-hour recall
options.D: Dietary record

explanation: Dietary records capture food intake in real-time, avoiding the memory errors common in retrospective recall methods. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h5)

question: Which clinical condition results from a dietary deficiency of iron?

options.A: Scurvy
options.B: Goiter
options.C: Rickets
options.D: Anemia

explanation: Iron deficiency impairs hemoglobin synthesis, resulting in anemia and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity in the blood. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h6)

question: Why are excessive doses of fat-soluble vitamins more likely to cause toxicity than water-soluble vitamins?

options.A: They accumulate in body tissues instead of being excreted in urine
options.B: They prevent the absorption of all dietary minerals
options.C: They bind directly to red blood cells and cause immediate clotting
options.D: They destroy beneficial gut bacteria required for digestion

explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and adipose tissue, making it easy for high quantities to build up to toxic levels. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h6)

question: Why do Nigerian dietary guidelines focus on combining local staples like grains and legumes?

options.A: To reduce the cooking time required for traditional dishes
options.B: To eliminate the need for agricultural farming of livestock
options.C: To achieve complete amino acid profiles using affordable foods
options.D: To comply with international export regulations for agriculture

explanation: Combining plant-based staples provides all essential amino acids together, offering an economical solution against protein-energy malnutrition. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h7)

question: Which public health issue remains a major concern driving nutritional education in Nigerian communities?

options.A: Protein-energy malnutrition
options.B: Excessive fiber intake
options.C: Hypervitaminosis toxicity
options.D: Celiac disease outbreaks

explanation: Protein-energy malnutrition affects vulnerable populations in Nigeria, making community-level nutritional guidance essential for nurses. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h7)

question: What happens when energy intake is greater than energy expenditure?

options.A: Energy stores are depleted for fuel
options.B: Metabolic rate drops to zero immediately
options.C: Body weight remains completely unchanged
options.D: Body weight increases due to fat storage

explanation: Extra energy consumed beyond what the body uses is stored in adipose tissue, leading to weight gain over time. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h1)

question: Why is energy balance compared to a bank account?

options.A: Because nutritional value is measured in monetary units
options.B: Because metabolic processes require physical currency
options.C: Because calories can be saved in a literal bank
options.D: Because deposits must equal withdrawals to maintain stability

explanation: Just like a bank balance, body weight reflects the net difference between what goes in and what comes out. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h1)

question: Which macronutrient provides the highest amount of energy per gram?

options.A: Vitamins
options.B: Proteins
options.C: Fats
options.D: Carbohydrates

explanation: Fats yield nine kilocalories per gram, which is more than double the energy density of carbohydrates or proteins. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h2)

question: A patient consumes a meal with zero calories. Which nutrient group does it most likely contain?

options.A: Dietary fats
options.B: Animal proteins
options.C: Vitamins and minerals
options.D: Complex carbohydrates

explanation: Vitamins, minerals, and water do not provide caloric energy, unlike carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h2)

question: What is the largest component of total daily energy expenditure for most people?

options.A: Basal metabolic rate
options.B: Spontaneous muscle twitching
options.C: Thermic effect of food
options.D: Planned physical exercise

explanation: Basal metabolic rate consumes the majority of daily energy, keeping vital organs functioning even at rest. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h3)

question: A bedridden patient has an energy expenditure primarily driven by which factor?

options.A: Basal metabolic rate
options.B: Scheduled sports activities
options.C: High thermic food processing
options.D: Voluntary skeletal movement

explanation: When physical activity is minimal, basal metabolism accounts for almost all of the body's daily energy usage. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h3)

question: What is the main difference between BMR and RMR measurements?

options.A: BMR includes physical activity while RMR does not
options.B: RMR applies only to animals rather than humans
options.C: RMR is measured under less strict resting conditions than BMR
options.D: BMR measures calorie intake instead of calorie output

explanation: BMR requires strict laboratory conditions after an overnight fast, whereas RMR is more casually measured under normal rest. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h4)

question: Why does a patient with high muscle mass have a higher resting metabolic rate?

options.A: Muscle tissue requires more energy to maintain than fat tissue
options.B: Muscle cells actively contract all night during sleep
options.C: Strong muscles prevent any heat loss from the skin
options.D: Muscles store excess vitamins that boost heat production

explanation: Muscle is metabolically active tissue that burns more calories at rest compared to adipose tissue. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h4)

question: Which macronutrient has the highest thermic effect of food?

options.A: Dietary fats
options.B: Saturated oils
options.C: Simple sugars
options.D: Protein

explanation: The body uses more energy to process and metabolize proteins than it does for carbohydrates or fats. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h5)

question: What does non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) include?

options.A: Basal metabolic processes during deep sleep
options.B: Everyday movements like standing, walking, and fidgeting
options.C: Intense weightlifting sessions at the local gym
options.D: The energy used to digest a heavy lunch

explanation: NEAT captures all the calories burned through routine daily actions outside of formal, structured exercise programs. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h5)

question: When is a positive energy balance considered a normal physiological necessity?

options.A: During prolonged starvation periods
options.B: During pregnancy and childhood growth
options.C: Throughout a fever or malaria infection
options.D: When treating severe acute dehydration

explanation: Growing bodies and pregnancies require extra energy and building blocks, making positive energy balance essential. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h6)

question: What is a primary risk of maintaining a severe negative energy balance for too long?

options.A: Increased resting metabolic rate and vitality
options.B: Rapid expansion of healthy fat tissue stores
options.C: Muscle wasting and nutritional deficiencies
options.D: Excessive bone density and mineral buildup

explanation: When intake falls too short of needs for too long, the body breaks down its own muscle and misses key nutrients. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h6)

question: What does indirect calorimetry measure to calculate energy expenditure?

options.A: Circulating blood glucose and lipid profiles
options.B: Direct body heat radiated inside a sealed room
options.C: Oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production
options.D: Total fluid intake versus urinary output volume

explanation: Indirect calorimetry estimates heat production by analyzing the gases a person breathes in and out. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h7)

question: Why do most general hospital wards rely on predictive equations rather than direct calorimetry?

options.A: Direct calorimetry can only be used on recovering surgical patients
options.B: Predictive equations measure actual heat output in real-time
options.C: Direct calorimetry is completely inaccurate for human subjects
options.D: Predictive equations are practical and require no special sealed chambers

explanation: Direct calorimetry requires complex, expensive laboratory rooms, making simple mathematical formulas much more accessible. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h7)

question: What is a common complication of severely underfeeding a hospitalized patient?

options.A: Delayed wound healing and muscle wasting
options.B: Rapid accumulation of excess adipose tissue
options.C: Acute fatty liver disease and high blood sugar
options.D: Dangerous fluid overload in the lung cavities

explanation: Insufficient energy and nutrient intake deprives the body of resources needed to repair tissues and maintain muscle mass. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h8)

question: Why must nurses carefully track and record a patient's daily meal intake?

options.A: To satisfy administrative paperwork requirements for the hospital board
options.B: To calculate the exact financial cost of hospital catering services
options.C: To help identify potential energy imbalances before complications arise
options.D: To determine how much physical exercise the patient did yesterday

explanation: Accurate intake records allow the care team to spot undernutrition or overfeeding early and adjust the care plan. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h8)

question: What occurs during a state of positive energy balance?

options.A: Stored body fat is mobilized for primary fuel
options.B: Body weight remains completely stable over time
options.C: Energy intake exceeds daily energy expenditure
options.D: Energy expenditure exceeds dietary consumption

explanation: Positive energy balance happens when you take in more calories than your body burns, leading to weight gain. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h1)

question: A patient losing weight consistently is experiencing which type of energy balance?

options.A: Neutral energy balance
options.B: Basal energy balance
options.C: Negative energy balance
options.D: Positive energy balance

explanation: Weight loss means the body is burning more energy than it receives from food, creating a negative balance. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h1)

question: One kilocalorie is roughly equal to how many kilojoules?

options.A: 9.00 kilojoules
options.B: 4.184 kilojoules
options.C: 2.25 kilojoules
options.D: 10.5 kilojoules

explanation: The standard conversion factor for food energy is one kilocalorie equaling about 4.184 kilojoules. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h2)

question: Why is the kilocalorie preferred over the joule in everyday clinical charting?

options.A: It represents a smaller amount of energy than a joule
options.B: It is the traditional unit most patients and clinicians recognize
options.C: It is the officially mandated global SI unit
options.D: It requires complex mathematical conversions to use

explanation: Kilocalories remain widely used because food labels and clinical habits have historically relied on them. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h2)

question: Which macronutrient yields the highest amount of energy per gram?

options.A: Carbohydrates
options.B: Fats
options.C: Vitamins
options.D: Proteins

explanation: Fats provide about 9 kilocalories per gram, making them more than twice as dense as carbs or proteins. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h3)

question: How many total calories are provided by a snack containing 10 grams of carbohydrate and 5 grams of fat?

options.A: 85 calories
options.B: 125 calories
options.C: 45 calories
options.D: 65 calories

explanation: Multiply 10 grams of carbs by 4 to get 40, and 5 grams of fat by 9 to get 45; adding them gives 85 calories. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h3)

question: What is the largest component of total daily energy expenditure in most sedentary individuals?

options.A: Basal metabolic rate
options.B: Thermic effect of food
options.C: Planned physical exercise
options.D: Adaptive thermogenesis

explanation: Basal metabolic rate typically accounts for the majority of the energy your body burns every day. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h4)

question: The energy required by the body to digest and process ingested food is called what?

options.A: Resting metabolic rate
options.B: Active caloric expenditure
options.C: Basal metabolic rate
options.D: Thermic effect of food

explanation: The thermic effect of food reflects the metabolic cost of processing the meals you eat. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h4)

question: Which diagnostic technique is considered the gold standard for measuring exact energy expenditure?

options.A: Skinfold thickness measurement
options.B: Harris-Benedict formula
options.C: Indirect calorimetry
options.D: Body mass index charting

explanation: Indirect calorimetry measures gas exchange to calculate actual energy expenditure with high precision. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h5)

question: Why might predictive equations like Harris-Benedict give inaccurate calorie targets for a patient with severe sepsis?

options.A: They rely exclusively on height rather than body weight
options.B: They measure expired gases instead of actual dietary intake
options.C: They only work for patients who are actively exercising
options.D: They fail to account for increased metabolic demands from fever and stress

explanation: Severe illness and fever spike metabolic rates beyond standard predictive formulas, requiring clinical adjustments. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h5)

question: What is a primary clinical consequence of prolonged negative energy balance in a hospitalized patient?

options.A: Elevated resting blood pressure levels
options.B: Delayed wound healing and muscle wasting
options.C: Immediate development of type 2 diabetes
options.D: Rapid expansion of adipose tissue stores

explanation: A prolonged lack of sufficient calories forces the body to break down muscle tissue and impairs healing processes. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h6)

question: Which health condition is most directly associated with long-term positive energy balance?

options.A: Marasmus
options.B: Obesity
options.C: Cachexia
options.D: Kwashiorkor

explanation: Consuming more calories than expended over a long period leads to excess fat accumulation, known as obesity. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h6)

question: What is a key responsibility of the nurse when managing a patient's nutritional care plan?

options.A: Monitoring daily food intake and tracking accurate body weights
options.B: Diagnosing underlying metabolic endocrine disorders
options.C: Calculating precise micronutrient molecular structures
options.D: Prescribing specialized parenteral nutrition formulas independently

explanation: Nurses track daily intake and weights to evaluate whether the nutritional plan is working effectively. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h7)

question: Why must a nurse consider local food availability and cultural preferences when providing dietary education?

options.A: It ensures the patient can realistically follow the dietary plan at home
options.B: It replaces the need for clinical supervision by a doctor
options.C: It eliminates the need for any calculated caloric goals
options.D: It prevents the patient from ever experiencing illness again

explanation: Dietary advice must be practical and culturally appropriate for patients to adopt and sustain long-term. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h7)

question: What does total daily energy expenditure measure in the human body?

options.A: Percentage of body fat stored in adipose tissue compartments
options.B: Total calories burned for all physiological and physical activities
options.C: Calories consumed through daily dietary intake and fluid consumption
options.D: Energy used exclusively during intense athletic training sessions

explanation: Total daily energy expenditure encompasses all energy used for basal functions, digestion, and movement throughout the day. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h1)

question: Why is understanding energy expenditure important for a clinical nurse?

options.A: It guides proper nutritional planning and metabolic support for patients
options.B: It replaces the need for routine vital sign monitoring on the ward
options.C: It determines the precise blood volume required for laboratory tests
options.D: It accurately predicts the exact date of a patient hospital discharge

explanation: Knowing energy expenditure helps nurses and dietitians calculate precise caloric requirements for healing and weight management. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h1)

question: What condition is required to accurately measure basal metabolic rate?

options.A: Complete physical rest after an overnight fast in a neutral environment
options.B: Light aerobic exercise performed immediately prior to the measurement
options.C: Active movement during a standardized treadmill walking test
options.D: Consumption of a high-protein meal one hour before testing

explanation: BMR must be measured when the body is at absolute rest and post-absorptive to eliminate digestive influences. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h2)

question: A bodybuilder typically has a higher resting metabolic rate than a sedentary person of the same weight because...

options.A: Frequent physical exercise permanently raises core body temperature
options.B: Muscle tissue burns more calories at rest than fat tissue
options.C: Digesting heavy protein diets requires continuous organ activity
options.D: Endocrine glands secrete extra hormones during heavy weightlifting

explanation: Lean muscle mass is metabolically active tissue that requires more energy to maintain than adipose tissue. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h2)

question: Which macronutrient has the highest thermic effect of food?

options.A: Simple sugars
options.B: Lipids
options.C: Complex starches
options.D: Protein

explanation: Protein demands significantly more metabolic energy for breakdown and processing than fats or carbohydrates. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h3)

question: What biological process primarily accounts for the thermic effect of food?

options.A: The metabolic cost of digestion, absorption, and nutrient processing
options.B: Heat produced by muscle contractions during the act of chewing
options.C: Friction generated by food moving rapidly through the intestinal tract
options.D: Thermal energy released when stomach acid dissolves food particles

explanation: The body expends active energy to break down food molecules and transport them across the intestinal mucosa. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h3)

question: What does the term NEAT stand for in metabolism studies?

options.A: Natural Elevation of Arterial Tension
options.B: Normal Endocrine Activation Time
options.C: Nutritional Energy Absorption Total
options.D: Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis

explanation: NEAT captures all the casual movement calories burned outside of dedicated athletic exercise. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h4)

question: An office worker who fidgets constantly and walks during breaks burns more daily calories than a stationary colleague mainly through increased...

options.A: Non-exercise activity thermogenesis
options.B: Thermic effect of food processing
options.C: Basal metabolic rate acceleration
options.D: Obligatory thermoregulatory output

explanation: Unconscious daily movements add up to a substantial variation in daily caloric burn between individuals. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h4)

question: What hormonal condition is most directly associated with a suppressed metabolic rate?

options.A: Diabetes mellitus
options.B: Hypothyroidism
options.C: Cushing syndrome
options.D: Hyperthyroidism

explanation: Inadequate thyroid hormone output slows cellular metabolism and reduces basal energy expenditure. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h5)

question: Why does basal metabolic rate naturally decrease as people grow older?

options.A: Gradual loss of active skeletal muscle mass over time
options.B: Permanent thickening of the outer layer of skin cells
options.C: Decreased fluid intake during the later decades of life
options.D: Slower secretion of digestive enzymes in the small intestine

explanation: Sarcopenia reduces metabolically active tissue, which lowers the baseline calories burned at rest. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h5)

question: What gas exchange values does indirect calorimetry measure to estimate energy expenditure?

options.A: Methane elimination and atmospheric pressure
options.B: Oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production
options.C: Carbon monoxide release and ambient humidity
options.D: Nitrogen excretion and hydrogen gas accumulation

explanation: Indirect calorimetry calculates metabolic rate by analyzing the volumes of oxygen consumed and carbon dioxide exhaled. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h6)

question: Why are predictive equations like Mifflin-St Jeor commonly used instead of direct calorimetry in routine hospital wards?

options.A: They eliminate the need to calculate physical activity levels completely
options.B: They measure actual physical heat loss more accurately than specialized chambers
options.C: They provide quick estimates using basic patient measurements without complex equipment
options.D: They automatically adjust for sudden changes in medication dosages

explanation: Predictive formulas offer a practical, cost-effective way to estimate caloric needs at the bedside. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h6)

question: A severely burned patient in the surgical ward experiences hypermetabolism, which means the nurse must anticipate...

options.A: A sharp decrease in core body temperature and basal metabolic rate
options.B: Minimal need for nutritional support due to complete physical rest
options.C: Significantly increased caloric and protein requirements for wound healing
options.D: Immediate conversion of excess dietary carbohydrates into stored fat

explanation: Major trauma and burns trigger a hypermetabolic response that sharply elevates daily energy expenditure. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h7)

question: What potential complication can occur when a critically ill patient is overfed with excessive carbohydrates?

options.A: Sudden electrolyte imbalance characterized by severe hypernatremia and dehydration
options.B: Increased carbon dioxide production that complicates weaning from mechanical ventilation
options.C: Permanent cessation of the thermic effect of food processing
options.D: Rapid expansion of skeletal muscle tissue replacing lost adipose stores

explanation: Excess carbohydrate intake increases the respiratory quotient and carbon dioxide output, straining breathing in compromised patients. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h7)

question: What primary nutrient do green leafy vegetables supply that helps prevent neural tube defects?

options.A: Folate
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Potassium
options.D: Vitamin C

explanation: Folate is a B vitamin concentrated in green leaves that is vital for DNA synthesis and preventing neural tube defects during fetal development. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h1)

question: How does dietary fiber from vegetables improve overall digestive health?

options.A: By providing direct energy to cardiac muscle tissues
options.B: By stimulating regular bowel movements and gut motility
options.C: By increasing the absorption rate of simple sugars
options.D: By blocking the breakdown of dietary proteins in the stomach

explanation: Fiber adds bulk to stool and stimulates movement through the gut, which prevents constipation and maintains a healthy digestive tract. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h1)

question: Which vegetable category includes cabbage, broccoli, and cauliflower?

options.A: Cruciferous
options.B: Bulb
options.C: Root
options.D: Tuber

explanation: Cruciferous vegetables belong to the Brassicaceae family and are characterized by specific sulfur-containing compounds called glucosinolates. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h2)

question: Why are tomatoes and garden eggs classified as fruit vegetables in nutrition?

options.A: They lack any significant vitamin or mineral content
options.B: They grow entirely underneath the soil surface
options.C: They possess woody stems similar to forest trees
options.D: They develop from the flower and contain seeds

explanation: Botanically, any plant structure that develops from a flower and contains seeds is a fruit, even if it is used in savory cooking. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h2)

question: What is the general daily minimum target for fruits and vegetables recommended for adults?

options.A: 50 grams
options.B: 100 grams
options.C: 400 grams
options.D: 1000 grams

explanation: Major health organizations establish the 400-gram daily minimum to safeguard against chronic illnesses and vitamin shortfalls. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h3)

question: A healthy adult should aim for approximately how many cups of vegetables per day?

options.A: 0.5 to 1 cup
options.B: 8 to 10 cups
options.C: 5 to 6 cups
options.D: 2.5 to 3 cups

explanation: Standard nutritional targets place adult vegetable needs between 2.5 and 3 cups daily depending on caloric intake and activity level. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h3)

question: What is the local name for the fluted pumpkin vegetable commonly consumed in Nigeria?

options.A: Gbure
options.B: Ugwu
options.C: Tete
options.D: Shoko

explanation: Ugwu is the vernacular term for fluted pumpkin leaves, a staple green vegetable rich in iron and folate across many Nigerian homes. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h4)

question: Why is promoting indigenous vegetables like Efo Tete and Shoko clinically beneficial in community nursing?

options.A: They are affordable, culturally accepted, and rich in micronutrients
options.B: They possess high amounts of complex animal proteins
options.C: They replace the need for drinking clean water during meals
options.D: They eliminate all risks of foodborne parasitic infections

explanation: Local accessibility and cultural familiarity make indigenous vegetables practical solutions for fighting malnutrition in community settings. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h4)

question: Which cooking method helps retain water-soluble vitamins best by minimizing water contact?

options.A: Steaming
options.B: Prolonged boiling
options.C: Deep frying
options.D: Soaking in water

explanation: Steaming cooks vegetables using steam vapor rather than submerging them in water, which prevents water-soluble vitamins from leaching away. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h5)

question: Why is incorporating a small amount of healthy oil beneficial when eating cooked green vegetables?

options.A: It stops the natural production of dietary fiber
options.B: It enhances the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
options.C: It converts vegetable carbohydrates into pure protein
options.D: It completely destroys all remaining harmful bacteria

explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins like vitamin A and K require dietary fats to be properly absorbed through the intestinal wall into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h5)

question: Which factor most commonly contributes to the rapid spoilage of fresh vegetables in resource-limited settings?

options.A: Lack of adequate refrigeration facilities
options.B: High humidity levels in deep freezers
options.C: The absence of table salt in the kitchen
options.D: Excessive exposure to natural sunlight indoors

explanation: Without cold storage, fresh leafy vegetables wilt and spoil rapidly due to high respiration rates and microbial growth in tropical climates. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical barrier to adequate vegetable consumption?

options.A: Dislike of bitter tastes by children
options.B: Excessive availability of cold storage
options.C: High market prices for fresh produce
options.D: Seasonal scarcity during dry spells

explanation: Abundant cold storage actually preserves vegetables longer, making it a facilitator of intake rather than a barrier. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h6)

question: A patient with hypertension is receiving dietary counseling. Which mineral found abundantly in green vegetables should the nurse emphasize for blood pressure control?

options.A: Calcium
options.B: Sodium
options.C: Potassium
options.D: Iron

explanation: Potassium helps lower blood pressure by easing tension in blood vessel walls and helping the body excrete excess sodium. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h7)

question: How do high-fiber vegetables assist patients managing type 2 diabetes?

options.A: By converting excess blood sugar into stored body fat
options.B: By directly replacing the function of pancreatic insulin cells
options.C: By slowing glucose absorption and preventing rapid blood sugar spikes
options.D: By completely eliminating carbohydrates from the digestive tract

explanation: Dietary fiber delays gastric emptying and slows sugar absorption in the small intestine, resulting in more stable blood glucose levels. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h7)

question: What primary mineral found in fruits helps regulate blood pressure?

options.A: Magnesium
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Potassium
options.D: Sodium

explanation: Potassium assists in maintaining normal blood pressure by reducing the effects of sodium in the vascular system. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h1)

question: Why is dietary fibre from fruits important for the gastrointestinal tract?

options.A: It acts as the primary energy source for red blood cells
options.B: It directly destroys harmful bacteria in the stomach
options.C: It regulates bowel movements and prevents constipation
options.D: It stimulates the liver to produce more digestive bile

explanation: Fibre adds bulk to stool, facilitating smooth passage through the intestines and preventing sluggish bowel function. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h1)

question: What is the accepted average weight of a single standard fruit portion?

options.A: 200 grams
options.B: 150 grams
options.C: 80 grams
options.D: 50 grams

explanation: Global public health standards typically define one standard fruit or vegetable portion as approximately 80 grams. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h2)

question: A healthy adult patient asks how many fruit portions to eat daily. What is your best response?

options.A: Eat only one large fruit basket once a week
options.B: Aim for a minimum of two to three portions daily
options.C: Limit all fruit intake to avoid excess protein
options.D: Consume as many sweet tropical fruits as possible

explanation: Standard dietary guidelines recommend that adults consume at least two to three portions of fruit daily as part of a balanced diet. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h2)

question: What component of whole fruit is mostly lost during the extraction of clear fruit juice?

options.A: Natural water
options.B: Plant protein
options.C: Essential amino acids
options.D: Dietary fibre

explanation: Squeezing and straining fruit removes the pulp and skin where the majority of beneficial dietary fibre is stored. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h3)

question: Why does drinking fruit juice cause a faster blood sugar spike than eating whole fruit?

options.A: Cold juice temperatures accelerate intestinal enzyme activity
options.B: The human stomach cannot absorb solid food nutrients
options.C: Liquid juice delivers free sugars rapidly without structural fibre
options.D: Juice contains added synthetic glucose that digests instantly

explanation: Without fibre to slow digestion, the sugars in juice enter the bloodstream much faster than when trapped inside whole fruit cells. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h3)

question: Which local Nigerian fruit is particularly known for containing the digestive enzyme papain?

options.A: Soursop
options.B: Cashew
options.C: Pawpaw
options.D: Banana

explanation: Pawpaw contains papain, a natural proteolytic enzyme that aids in breaking down dietary proteins during digestion. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h4)

question: What is a major advantage of recommending seasonal local fruits to patients in Nigeria?

options.A: They are more affordable and retain higher nutrient levels
options.B: They contain zero natural sugars compared to imported options
options.C: They completely eliminate the need for drinking water
options.D: They can be stored at room temperature for several years

explanation: Local seasonal fruits require less storage and transport time, making them cheaper and fresher than imported alternatives. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h4)

question: Which strategy best helps a low-income patient increase their daily fruit intake?

options.A: Avoiding all perishable foods to save household money
options.B: Buying local fruits in season when market prices drop
options.C: Purchasing only imported organic berries from supermarkets
options.D: Relying exclusively on expensive vitamin C tablets

explanation: Purchasing seasonal local produce is the most cost-effective way to maintain adequate fruit intake on a limited budget. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended approach for managing fruit spoilage in tropical climates?

options.A: Utilizing frozen alternatives when fresh fruit is unavailable
options.B: Storing ripe fruits in cool, well-ventilated areas of the kitchen
options.C: Consuming seasonal produce promptly after purchase
options.D: Leaving fresh fruits sealed inside airtight plastic bags in the sun

explanation: Trapping fresh fruit in heat and airtight plastic accelerates moisture buildup, fungal growth, and rapid decay. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h5)

question: How many kilocalories of energy does one gram of dietary fat provide?

options.A: Nine kilocalories
options.B: Seven kilocalories
options.C: Twelve kilocalories
options.D: Four kilocalories

explanation: Lipids yield a higher caloric density per gram compared to carbohydrates and proteins, delivering nine kilocalories. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h1)

question: Why does the body need dietary fat to use fat-soluble vitamins?

options.A: Fats break down stomach acids to release vitamin molecules.
options.B: Fats act as a direct chemical precursor to create vitamins in the liver.
options.C: Fats provide the required medium for transporting and absorbing these vitamins.
options.D: Fats stimulate the pancreas to secrete active vitamin enzymes.

explanation: Vitamins A, D, E, and K depend on dietary lipids to cross the intestinal lining and circulate properly in the body. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h1)

question: Which type of fat contains multiple double carbon bonds and includes essential fatty acids?

options.A: Polyunsaturated fats
options.B: Hydrogenated fats
options.C: Trans fats
options.D: Saturated fats

explanation: Polyunsaturated fats possess two or more double bonds and include essential omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids that the body cannot make on its own. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h2)

question: Why are trans fats considered more harmful to heart health than other unsaturated fats?

options.A: They block the liver from metabolizing basic dietary carbohydrates.
options.B: They increase low-density lipoprotein cholesterol while reducing high-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
options.C: They prevent the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins in the small intestine.
options.D: They store excessive amounts of water within the subcutaneous adipose tissue.

explanation: Industrial trans fats negatively alter blood cholesterol by raising bad LDL cholesterol and lowering good HDL cholesterol at the same time. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h2)

question: What is the recommended daily percentage of total calories from fat for healthy adults?

options.A: Forty to fifty percent
options.B: Sixty to seventy percent
options.C: Ten to fifteen percent
options.D: Twenty to thirty-five percent

explanation: Health guidelines recommend that twenty to thirty-five percent of a healthy adult's daily energy come from fats. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h3)

question: What is the main nutritional recommendation regarding trans fat intake?

options.A: Keep intake as close to zero as possible
options.B: Obtain trans fats strictly from plant-based sources
options.C: Match trans fat intake equally with saturated fat intake
options.D: Keep intake below ten percent of daily calories

explanation: Because artificial trans fats offer no health benefits and carry serious heart risks, health authorities advise keeping intake near zero. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h3)

question: Which health condition is strongly linked to a long-term excess of dietary trans and saturated fats?

options.A: Atherosclerosis
options.B: Osteomalacia
options.C: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
options.D: Pernicious anemia

explanation: Eating too many unhealthy fats raises blood cholesterol, which leads to plaque buildup and narrowing of the arteries. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h4)

question: What physical sign is commonly seen in a patient with a severe lack of essential fatty acids?

options.A: Yellowing of the sclera and mucous membranes
options.B: Rapid and unexpected weight gain
options.C: Dry, scaly skin and poor wound healing
options.D: Severe stiffness in the large weight-bearing joints

explanation: Essential fatty acid deficiency weakens cell membranes in the skin, leading to dryness, rashes, and delayed tissue repair. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h4)

question: Which food substitution best supports a heart-healthy diet for a patient with high cholesterol?

options.A: Replacing palm oil with liquid vegetable oils like olive or groundnut oil
options.B: Replacing fresh fruits with canned fruits packed in heavy syrup
options.C: Replacing lean poultry with processed red meat products
options.D: Replacing whole grains with refined white flour products

explanation: Swapping solid saturated fats for liquid plant oils helps lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h5)

question: A patient wants to eat more omega-3 fatty acids. Which food should the nurse recommend?

options.A: Refined corn oil
options.B: Polished white rice
options.C: Oily fish like mackerel
options.D: White bread

explanation: Mackerel and other oily fish are rich, natural sources of heart-healthy omega-3 polyunsaturated fats. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h5)

question: What is the primary function of dietary glucose in the human body?

options.A: Repairing damaged muscle fibers
options.B: Building strong bone matrices
options.C: Regulating fluid electrolyte balance
options.D: Providing quick cellular energy

explanation: Glucose serves as a primary fuel source for cellular respiration and metabolic processes throughout the body. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h1)

question: Which sugar is classified as a monosaccharide?

options.A: Sucrose
options.B: Maltose
options.C: Lactose
options.D: Fructose

explanation: Fructose is a single-molecule sugar, making it a monosaccharide, whereas the others are disaccharides. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h1)

question: Why do intrinsic sugars digest slower than free sugars?

options.A: They lack any chemical bonds requiring breakdown
options.B: They bypass the stomach and enter the colon directly
options.C: They require specialized pancreatic enzymes to function
options.D: They are bound within whole cellular fruit matrices

explanation: Intrinsic sugars are trapped inside plant cell walls, slowing digestion and preventing rapid blood glucose spikes. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h2)

question: Which category includes honey and maple syrup consumed in diets?

options.A: Complex starches
options.B: Intrinsic sugars
options.C: Free sugars
options.D: Structural fibers

explanation: Honey and syrups are classified as free sugars because they are not enclosed within cellular plant walls. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h2)

question: A patient with chronic high sugar intake develops insulin resistance. What is the primary mechanism?

options.A: Downregulation of cellular insulin receptors
options.B: Increased renal excretion of glucose molecules
options.C: Destruction of the pancreatic beta cells
options.D: Accelerated breakdown of circulating insulin

explanation: Constant high levels of insulin and glucose cause cell receptors to become less responsive over time. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h3)

question: Which organ is primarily responsible for metabolizing dietary fructose?

options.A: Pancreas
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Liver
options.D: Stomach

explanation: The liver processes the vast majority of dietary fructose, turning excess amounts into triglycerides. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h3)

question: What is the primary WHO threshold for daily free sugar intake in adults?

options.A: Less than 10% of total energy intake
options.B: Up to 20% of total daily protein intake
options.C: No more than 2 teaspoons per meal
options.D: Exactly 50 grams for all body weights

explanation: The WHO guideline strongly advises keeping free sugars below 10% of total daily calories to prevent disease. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h4)

question: Why does the WHO suggest a conditional further reduction of sugars to 5%?

options.A: To provide additional protection against dental caries and obesity
options.B: To ensure adequate total vitamin absorption in the gut
options.C: To completely eliminate carbohydrates from human metabolism
options.D: To compensate for the lack of exercise in modern cities

explanation: Dropping below 5% offers extra health benefits, particularly regarding tooth decay and weight management. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h4)

question: A patient reads a food label and sees maltodextrin and dextrose. What do these represent?

options.A: Artificial sweeteners with zero calories
options.B: Hidden forms of added dietary sugars
options.C: Essential amino acids for tissue repair
options.D: Complex dietary fibers for bowel motility

explanation: Terms ending in '-ose' or words like maltodextrin are various chemical names for hidden added sugars. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h5)

question: What is the purpose of food manufacturers splitting sugar types on ingredient lists?

options.A: To improve the overall vitamin content of the snack
options.B: To help diabetic patients calculate accurate insulin doses
options.C: To comply with international public health labeling laws
options.D: To make added sugars appear further down the list

explanation: Using different names prevents a single sugar category from dominating the top of the ingredient list. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h5)

question: A patient wants to reduce sugar intake but struggles with sweet cravings after dinner. What is a suitable nursing recommendation?

options.A: Replacing meals entirely with black coffee
options.B: Eating a portion of whole fresh fruit
options.C: Eliminating all carbohydrates from the diet

options.A: To determine the hospital's electrical power generation needs
