options.C: To force patients to abandon traditional eating practices
options.D: To offer realistic dietary advice that respects patient beliefs

explanation: Dietary recommendations must align with cultural and religious norms to ensure the patient actually follows them. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h5)

question: Which body tissues usually show signs of nutrient deficiencies first?

options.A: Deep skeletal bone structures
options.B: Major internal cardiac valves
options.C: Large cortical brain regions
options.D: Skin, hair, and oral mucosa

explanation: Tissues with high cell turnover rates display nutritional deficits rapidly compared to more stable tissues. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h6)

question: What does the presence of muscle wasting and swollen gums suggest during a nutritional assessment?

options.A: Underlying protein and vitamin deficiencies
options.B: Excessive daily physical exercise
options.C: Adequate caloric and fluid intake
options.D: Normal physiological aging processes

explanation: Wasting muscles and inflamed mucous membranes are classic physical signs of insufficient protein and vitamin intake. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h6)

question: What is the primary benefit of accurate nutritional documentation in the patient chart?

options.A: Providing legal protection against medication calculation errors
options.B: Eliminating the need for verbal shift handover reports
options.C: Ensuring continuity of care across different shifts and staff
options.D: Reducing the overall duration of hospital stay

explanation: Clear records allow every healthcare provider involved to understand the patient's nutritional status and plan. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h7)

question: How do analyzed nutritional findings assist the nursing team?

options.A: They determine hospital room assignments and bed counts
options.B: They automatically generate pharmacy prescription refills
options.C: They help establish formal nursing diagnoses for care planning
options.D: They replace the physician's medical diagnosis entirely

explanation: Processed data leads to specific nursing diagnoses that drive targeted interventions and evaluation strategies. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h7)

question: Which strategy helps nurses obtain more accurate portion size estimates during a diet history?

options.A: Asking closed yes-or-no questions about food weight
options.B: Using visual aids like food models or local household measures
options.C: Demanding exact laboratory measurements for every meal
options.D: Relying solely on standardized hospital kitchen scales

explanation: Visual props help patients picture portion sizes better than abstract measurements alone. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h8)

question: What approach should a nurse take when a patient appears hesitant to report poor eating habits?

options.A: Document that the patient is intentionally non-compliant
options.B: Maintain non-judgmental communication and use open-ended questions
options.C: Scold the patient to ensure they tell the absolute truth
options.D: Skip the nutritional assessment entirely to save time

explanation: Creating a safe, welcoming environment encourages patients to share honest dietary habits without fear of criticism. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h8)

question: What does anthropometric assessment primarily measure in a clinical setting?

options.A: Body size, weight, and proportions
options.B: Electrical activity of the heart
options.C: Serum electrolyte and protein levels
options.D: Oxygen saturation in peripheral tissues

explanation: Anthropometry focuses entirely on physical dimensions like height, weight, and circumferences to evaluate nutritional health. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h1)

question: Why is anthropometry heavily utilized in resource-limited healthcare facilities in Nigeria?

options.A: It is non-invasive, cost-effective, and rapid
options.B: It requires expensive and specialized digital machinery
options.C: It replaces the need for any laboratory testing
options.D: It provides definitive diagnostic pathology reports

explanation: Simple physical measurements require minimal equipment, making them ideal for quick screening where advanced diagnostics are scarce. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h1)

question: What is the primary action a nurse must take before weighing a patient on a beam balance scale?

options.A: Calibrate the scale using heavy metal weights
options.B: Cover the weighing surface with thick fabric
options.C: Sanitize the platform with strong bleach
options.D: Ensure the scale is balanced at zero

explanation: Zeroing the scale prevents baseline errors and ensures the recorded weight reflects only the patient. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h2)

question: Why must measuring tapes used for anthropometry be made of non-stretchable material?

options.A: To ensure the tape changes length with body temperature
options.B: To allow the tape to wrap around curved joints easily
options.C: To prevent measurement distortion over time
options.D: To make the tape safe for use on open wounds

explanation: Cloth or stretching plastic tapes warp with repeated pulling, giving false readings for waist and arm circumferences. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h2)

question: How should a patient's head be positioned when measuring standing height?

options.A: Turned completely toward the right shoulder
options.B: Tilted back to look directly at the ceiling
options.C: Flexed forward with the chin touching the chest
options.D: Looking straight ahead with the line of sight parallel to the floor

explanation: Keeping the line of sight parallel to the floor maintains proper head alignment, ensuring an accurate and consistent height measurement. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h3)

question: A nurse is preparing to measure the length of a 14-month-old toddler. What equipment is required?

options.A: A rigid recumbent length board
options.B: A hanging spring balance scale
options.C: A standard vertical wall stadiometer
options.D: A flexible tailoring measuring tape

explanation: Children under two years old cannot stand reliably, so recumbent length must be measured flat on a specialized board. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h3)

question: What two body parameters are required to calculate a patient's Body Mass Index?

options.A: Age and waist size
options.B: Height and arm span
options.C: Weight and blood pressure
options.D: Weight and height

explanation: BMI uses mass in kilograms divided by height in meters squared to estimate general body fatness. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h4)

question: What is a major limitation of using BMI as a sole indicator of body composition?

options.A: It cannot be calculated for adult females over age fifty
options.B: It only applies to individuals living in tropical climates
options.C: It does not differentiate between muscle and fat mass
options.D: It requires expensive laboratory blood work to verify

explanation: Dense muscle tissue weighs more than fat, causing muscular individuals to fall into higher BMI brackets inaccurately. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h4)

question: What does a low Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) primarily indicate in community health screenings?

options.A: Chronic systemic hypertension
options.B: Severe dehydration and shock
options.C: Excess visceral adiposity
options.D: Severe acute malnutrition

explanation: MUAC is a trusted indicator of muscle wasting and undernutrition, especially in young children and pregnant mothers. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h5)

question: Where should the nurse locate the arm midpoint when measuring MUAC?

options.A: Between the acromion and olecranon processes
options.B: Just above the wrist bones on the forearm
options.C: One inch below the center of the armpit
options.D: Directly over the prominent elbow joint

explanation: The correct landmarking requires finding the halfway point between the shoulder tip and the elbow tip. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h5)

question: What tool do nurses use to visually track a child's growth patterns over time?

options.A: Daily fluid balance sheets
options.B: Serum lipid profiles
options.C: Body surface area graphs
options.D: WHO growth charts

explanation: Growth charts plot anthropometric values against standardized age curves to monitor pediatric development. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h6)

question: What does a downward crossing of percentile lines on a child's growth chart usually suggest?

options.A: Normal stabilization of skeletal length
options.B: Rapid and healthy adolescent maturation
options.C: Faltering growth or potential undernutrition
options.D: Temporary increase in physical activity

explanation: When a child drops across major percentile channels, it signals an interruption in normal development requiring evaluation. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T003#GNS227_U5_T003_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of a clinical nutritional assessment in nursing?

options.A: To calculate the exact daily food budget
options.B: To diagnose underlying gastrointestinal diseases
options.C: To determine the nutritional status of patients
options.D: To prescribe specific medical diets to patients

explanation: Nutritional assessment provides a systematic way to evaluate a patient's overall health and identify deficiencies. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h1)

question: Why is early detection of malnutrition crucial in hospital settings?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any laboratory tests
options.B: It prevents complications like delayed wound healing
options.C: it guarantees immediate discharge from the ward
options.D: It reduces the cost of hospital building maintenance

explanation: Catching nutritional risks early helps avoid severe issues such as slow recovery and higher infection rates. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h1)

question: A complete nutritional history must include information about recent changes in what measurement?

options.A: Arm span
options.B: Height growth
options.C: Shoe size
options.D: Body weight

explanation: Tracking unintentional weight gain or loss over a few months is a key indicator of nutritional trouble. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h2)

question: A patient reports severe difficulty swallowing during the nutritional interview. How should the nurse categorize this symptom?

options.A: A normal physiological sign of aging
options.B: A primary marker of high metabolic demand
options.C: An indication of excessive fluid retention
options.D: A gastrointestinal symptom limiting oral intake

explanation: Swallowing issues directly impede a patient's ability to ingest food safely and adequately. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h2)

question: Which vitamin deficiency is commonly indicated by the presence of Bitot's spots on the eyes?

options.A: Vitamin D
options.B: Vitamin K
options.C: Vitamin E
options.D: Vitamin A

explanation: Dry eyes and Bitot's spots are classic physical signs of inadequate vitamin A intake. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h3)

question: Why do physical signs of nutrient deficiency often appear first in tissues with rapid cell turnover?

options.A: Blood flow to the skin and hair is always slower
options.B: These tissues constantly require new cells and nutrients
options.C: They are more exposed to sunlight and air
options.D: They store more fat than internal organs do

explanation: Tissues like skin, hair, and mucosal linings divide quickly and show shortages faster than stable tissues. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h3)

question: What formula is used to calculate the Body Mass Index of an adult patient?

options.A: Weight in pounds divided by height in inches
options.B: Height in centimeters multiplied by weight in kilograms
options.C: Weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared
options.D: Arm circumference divided by total body surface area

explanation: BMI is standardly calculated using weight in kilograms over height squared in meters. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h4)

question: Mid-upper arm circumference is most valuable in community nursing for which reason?

options.A: It gives an exact percentage of total body water
options.B: It replaces the need to ever weigh the patient
options.C: It provides a quick and simple malnutrition screening
options.D: It measures the exact bone density of the arm

explanation: MUAC requires minimal equipment and time, making it ideal for rapid field assessments. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h4)

question: What effect does severe dehydration typically have on a patient's body weight and lab values during assessment?

options.A: It always causes a dramatic increase in muscle mass
options.B: It lowers all blood electrolyte levels instantly
options.C: It can falsely elevate lab values and distort weight readings
options.D: It has no impact on laboratory test results

explanation: Loss of plasma volume concentrates blood components, making lab values appear higher than they truly are. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h5)

question: Which clinical observation is a reliable sign of fluid volume deficit in an adult patient?

options.A: Bounding peripheral pulses and high blood pressure
options.B: Rapid weight gain over twenty-four hours
options.C: Sunken eyes and poor skin turgor
options.D: Pitting edema in the lower limbs

explanation: Dehydration reduces tissue elasticity and fluid volume around the eyes, showing up as poor turgor and sunken orbits. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h5)

question: Which serum protein is commonly measured to help evaluate a patient's visceral protein status?

options.A: Creatinine
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Bilirubin
options.D: Albumin

explanation: Serum albumin is a traditional biochemical marker used to assess protein levels in the body. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid relying solely on serum albumin to judge a patient's nutrition?

options.A: Inflammation and stress can alter albumin levels independently of diet
options.B: Albumin is only found in animal muscle tissue
options.C: The laboratory test takes several weeks to process
options.D: Albumin levels never change during a hospital stay

explanation: Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant, meaning illness or injury drops its level even if nutrition is adequate. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of documenting nutritional assessment findings in the nursing notes?

options.A: To ensure continuity of care among healthcare team members
options.B: To replace the need for verbal shift handovers
options.C: To fulfill legal requirements without reading them later
options.D: To calculate monthly hospital food expenses

explanation: Clear documentation allows all shifts and disciplines to track the patient's nutritional progress accurately. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h7)

question: Which element is essential when writing a nutritional nursing care plan?

options.A: Measurable goals for weight or intake
options.B: A guarantee of complete recovery within two days
options.C: Strict dietary restrictions for all family visitors
options.D: Exclusive reliance on intravenous nutrition

explanation: Care plans require concrete, measurable objectives to evaluate if the interventions are actually improving the patient's status. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T004#GNS227_U5_T004_h7)

question: What is the primary advantage of biochemical assessment over dietary histories in clinical practice?

options.A: It takes less time to perform
options.B: It costs significantly less money
options.C: It avoids subjective reporting errors
options.D: It relies on patient memory

explanation: Biochemical tests use objective laboratory measurements instead of depending on what a patient remembers or reports about their diet. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h1)

question: A patient shows no physical signs of malnutrition yet laboratory values indicate a deficiency. Why does this occur?

options.A: Biochemical tests can detect early nutritional imbalances before physical symptoms develop
options.B: The patient's body has already fully compensated for the missing nutrients
options.C: Physical examinations are completely useless for detecting protein malnutrition
options.D: Laboratory errors frequently happen during routine hospital blood sample collections

explanation: Laboratory markers drop during the early stages of depletion long before visible clinical signs appear on the body. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h1)

question: A test that measures the actual concentration of a nutrient in blood plasma is known as what?

options.A: A clinical assessment
options.B: A static biomarker
options.C: A functional biomarker
options.D: An anthropometric index

explanation: Static tests directly measure the absolute amount of a nutrient present within a biological fluid or tissue sample. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h2)

question: Measuring enzyme activity that depends on a specific vitamin cofactor is an example of which assessment type?

options.A: A static nutritional test
options.B: An anthropometric body measurement
options.C: A routine hematological screening
options.D: A functional nutritional test

explanation: Functional tests evaluate the physiological impact or metabolic consequences resulting from a shortage of a specific nutrient. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h2)

question: Which visceral protein marker has the shortest half-life, making it useful for tracking short-term changes?

options.A: Serum prealbumin
options.B: Plasma transferrin
options.C: Total protein
options.D: Serum albumin

explanation: Prealbumin has a rapid half-life of two to three days, allowing it to reflect recent dietary protein improvements quickly. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h3)

question: Why is serum albumin considered a poor indicator of acute nutritional depletion?

options.A: It disappears completely from the bloodstream within twenty-four hours
options.B: It has a long half-life and remains stable during early dietary inadequacy
options.C: It breaks down immediately when infection enters the human body
options.D: It only measures iron transport capacity rather than overall amino acids

explanation: Because albumin stays in the body for nearly three weeks, levels take a long time to drop even when protein intake stops. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h3)

question: What does serum calcium typically reflect when measured in a routine chemistry panel?

options.A: Immediate dietary consumption of dairy
options.B: Intracellular mineral storage capacity
options.C: Tight hormonal regulation rather than intake
options.D: Total skeletal bone density

explanation: The body tightly controls blood calcium levels using hormones, meaning serum numbers stay normal even when bone stores are depleted. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h4)

question: Why is relying on a single serum iron test insufficient for diagnosing iron deficiency?

options.A: Laboratories cannot accurately measure trace mineral amounts in blood
options.B: Serum iron levels never change during chronic inflammatory disease states
options.C: Serum iron fluctuates widely and does not show total body iron stores
options.D: Iron is stored exclusively inside red blood cells rather than plasma

explanation: Serum iron changes throughout the day and with recent meals, so clinicians need storage markers like ferritin to confirm a true deficit. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h4)

question: An elevated Mean Corpuscular Volume points toward a deficiency in which specific nutrients?

options.A: Vitamin C and zinc
options.B: Iron and copper
options.C: Calcium and magnesium
options.D: Vitamin B12 or folate

explanation: A high MCV indicates macrocytic red blood cells, which classically develop when vitamin B12 or folate is lacking. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h5)

question: A laboratory report shows microcytic anemia in a patient with chronic fatigue. What is the most likely underlying nutritional cause?

options.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency
options.B: Folate deficiency
options.C: Protein malnutrition
options.D: Iron deficiency

explanation: Microcytic anemia means the red blood cells are smaller than normal, which is the hallmark laboratory finding of iron shortage. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h5)

question: What happens to serum albumin levels during an acute inflammatory response in the body?

options.A: Levels increase significantly
options.B: Levels remain completely stable
options.C: Levels decrease significantly
options.D: Levels fluctuate unpredictably

explanation: Albumin acts as a negative acute-phase reactant, dropping rapidly when systemic inflammation or infection is present. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h6)

question: Why is checking C-reactive protein essential when interpreting a low serum prealbumin level?

options.A: It rules out any possibility of underlying iron deficiency anemia
options.B: It proves the patient is eating enough dietary protein daily
options.C: It measures the exact storage capacity of vitamins in the liver
options.D: It helps determine if low prealbumin is caused by inflammation rather than poor diet

explanation: Elevated C-reactive protein confirms that acute inflammation is suppressing visceral protein synthesis, preventing a false diagnosis of malnutrition. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h6)

question: What is the best approach when evaluating serial laboratory values for a hospitalized patient?

options.A: Average all available laboratory values together
options.B: Look only at the single most recent lab value
options.C: Evaluate trends in the data over a period of time
options.D: Compare the patient values to past hospital admissions

explanation: Following trends over time gives a much clearer picture of nutritional recovery or decline than looking at an isolated test result. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h7)

question: A patient receiving intravenous fluids shows a sudden drop in multiple serum nutrient concentrations. What factor should the nurse consider first?

options.A: Hemodilution caused by excess fluid administration
options.B: Severe laboratory error in processing the blood sample
options.C: Rapid consumption of nutrients by active tissue cells
options.D: Acute worsening of chronic dietary protein malnutrition

explanation: Excess intravenous fluids expand blood volume, diluting the concentration of circulating blood components without a true change in nutrient mass. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h7)

question: Which organ system dysfunction directly impairs the synthesis of key transport proteins used in nutritional assessment?

options.A: The endocrine system
options.B: The respiratory system
options.C: The renal system
options.D: The hepatic system

explanation: The liver synthesizes most circulating blood proteins, so hepatic disease directly interferes with these nutritional biomarker levels. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a confounding factor that can alter the interpretation of biochemical nutritional markers?

options.A: Normal biological hydration status
options.B: Underlying systemic liver disease
options.C: Presence of acute body inflammation
options.D: Standard daily physical exercise

explanation: Hydration changes, liver disease, and inflammation directly alter biomarker concentrations, whereas routine daily exercise does not confound baseline nutritional lab values in the same way. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T005#GNS227_U5_T005_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of a dietary assessment in clinical nursing?

options.A: Evaluating an individual's food and nutrient intake
options.B: Calculating the exact daily hospital food budget
options.C: Determining the patient's exact genetic metabolic rate
options.D: Prescribing specialized surgical diets without a doctor

explanation: Dietary assessment systematically measures what a person eats to understand their baseline nutrition. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h1)

question: Why is dietary assessment particularly crucial during initial nursing admissions?

options.A: It eliminates all risks of hospital-acquired infections
options.B: It guarantees the patient will follow hospital routines
options.C: It replaces the need for standard anthropometric measurements
options.D: It uncovers hidden nutrient deficits before physical symptoms appear

explanation: Catching inadequate intake early helps prevent full-blown malnutrition during a hospital stay. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h1)

question: Monitoring a therapeutic diet over time is a key objective of which nursing activity?

options.A: Intravenous line insertion
options.B: Routine blood transfusion
options.C: Surgical wound debridement
options.D: Dietary intake evaluation

explanation: Tracking food intake helps nurses see if a prescribed therapeutic diet is working. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h2)

question: How does dietary evaluation support community health epidemiology?

options.A: Determining the cost of pharmaceutical drugs nationwide
options.B: Treating acute malaria outbreaks in rural health posts
options.C: Linking food patterns to chronic diseases in populations
options.D: Mapping out safe drinking water sources in villages

explanation: Population-level dietary data helps researchers connect eating habits to disease trends. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h2)

question: What does a 24-hour dietary recall method require a patient to do?

options.A: Write down every ingredient before cooking a pot of soup
options.B: Report all foods and beverages consumed over the past day
options.C: Fast completely for a full day before laboratory blood tests
options.D: Weigh every single meal on a scale for an entire week

explanation: A 24-hour recall asks the patient to list everything eaten during the previous day. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h3)

question: A major drawback of retrospective dietary methods is their reliance on what factor?

options.A: Expensive laboratory kits
options.B: Strict surgical clearance
options.C: The patient's memory
options.D: Continuous ward admission

explanation: Since retrospective methods look backward, they depend entirely on what the patient can remember. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h3)

question: What is the primary characteristic of a prospective dietary assessment method?

options.A: Recording food intake as it happens in real time
options.B: Recalling meals eaten during childhood years
options.C: Estimating food portions five years after discharge
options.D: Guessing nutrient intake based on blood test results

explanation: Prospective methods capture data at the exact moment of consumption to avoid memory lapses. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h4)

question: Why can weighed food records be difficult to use in busy clinical wards?

options.A: They require continuous intravenous fluid therapy
options.B: They only work for patients who are completely blind
options.C: They place a high burden on staff and patients
options.D: They cannot be calculated using local food tables

explanation: Weighing every single item and leftover demands significant time and effort from patients and nurses. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h4)

question: What does the acronym RDA stand for in nutritional assessment?

options.A: Routine Daily Allocation
options.B: Rapid Dietary Assessment
options.C: Reference Disease Algorithm
options.D: Recommended Dietary Allowance

explanation: RDA stands for Recommended Dietary Allowance, representing intake levels that meet nearly all healthy individuals' needs. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h5)

question: Which DRI parameter represents the highest daily nutrient intake unlikely to cause harm?

options.A: Minimum Daily Requirement
options.B: Estimated Average Requirement
options.C: Recommended Dietary Allowance
options.D: Tolerable Upper Intake Level

explanation: The Tolerable Upper Intake Level defines the safe threshold before nutrient toxicity occurs. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h5)

question: Why do patients sometimes misreport their food intake during dietary assessments?

options.A: They want to impress the nurse with healthy choices
options.B: They want to speed up intravenous fluid removal
options.C: They are trying to reduce hospital admission fees
options.D: They are required by law to hide their recipes

explanation: Social desirability bias causes patients to underreport unhealthy items and exaggerate healthy ones. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h6)

question: Which factor makes assessing mixed Nigerian dishes particularly challenging?

options.A: Lack of any standard kitchen utensils throughout the country
options.B: The complete absence of local vegetables in traditional markets
options.C: Difficulty in measuring precise ingredient proportions in a shared pot
options.D: Strict legal regulations forbidding the analysis of soups

explanation: Mixed dishes contain varied ingredients cooked together, making exact nutrient breakdowns hard to calculate. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h6)

question: A patient's dietary record reveals extreme nutrient deficiencies. What is the appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Scold the patient for eating poor quality food at home
options.B: Collaborate with the dietitian to formulate a culturally appropriate meal plan
options.C: Discharge the patient immediately without further nutritional support
options.D: Stop all medication administration and start strict bed rest

explanation: Nurses use assessment findings to collaborate on practical, culturally relevant nutritional interventions. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h7)

question: How does the evaluation phase tie back into the initial dietary assessment?

options.A: By rewriting the hospital budget for kitchen supplies
options.B: By checking if weight changes and lab values show improvement
options.C: By closing the patient file and stopping all nursing notes
options.D: By ensuring the patient never eats local food again

explanation: Evaluating the care plan requires measuring clinical outcomes against baseline dietary data. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h7)

question: What is the primary characteristic of a fluid diet?

options.A: Consists entirely of liquids or foods melting at body temperature
options.B: Provides all daily caloric requirements for long-term feeding
options.C: Contains only high-protein supplements and raw vegetable juices
options.D: Includes soft, mashed solid foods that require minimal chewing

explanation: A fluid diet is strictly limited to items that are liquid at room or body temperature to accommodate impaired chewing or swallowing. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h1)

question: Why is a fluid diet typically prescribed as a temporary measure?

options.A: Hospital kitchen budgets cannot sustain liquid preparation
options.B: It lacks sufficient long-term nutritional value and calories
options.C: Patients quickly lose their taste for liquid meals
options.D: Solid food production is cheaper than liquid supplements

explanation: Fluid diets are low in energy and essential nutrients, making them inadequate for prolonged nutritional support. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h1)

question: A fluid diet is commonly ordered after abdominal surgery to achieve what goal?

options.A: Gently reintroduce foods while minimizing bowel stress
options.B: Force the bowels to empty completely within two hours
options.C: Provide maximum daily protein for rapid wound healing
options.D: Prevent the patient from feeling hungry too quickly

explanation: Post-operative patients receive fluids first because the bowel is sluggish and requires minimal digestive effort. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h2)

question: A stroke patient with swallowing difficulties is placed on a fluid diet primarily to prevent what complication?

options.A: Electrolyte overload
options.B: Rapid weight gain
options.C: Severe constipation
options.D: Aspiration pneumonia

explanation: Swallowing deficits put patients at high risk of choking or inhaling liquids into the lungs, leading to aspiration pneumonia. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h2)

question: Clear fluid diets are best distinguished by which feature?

options.A: You can see through the items at room temperature
options.B: They contain blended pieces of cooked vegetables
options.C: They provide complete daily vitamins and minerals
options.D: They are strictly limited to cold water and ice chips

explanation: Clear fluids are transparent liquids that leave virtually no undigested residue in the gastrointestinal tract. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h3)

question: What food item is allowed on a full fluid diet but NOT on a clear fluid diet?

options.A: Plain milk
options.B: Clear beef broth
options.C: Plain water
options.D: Apple juice

explanation: Milk is opaque and classified as a full fluid, whereas broths and juices are transparent enough for a clear fluid diet. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h3)

question: The main nutritional drawback of an unsupplemented clear fluid diet is deficiency in what?

options.A: Sodium and water
options.B: Simple sugars
options.C: Calories and protein
options.D: Fluid volume

explanation: Clear broths and teas lack the energy and building blocks necessary to maintain muscle mass and tissue repair. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h4)

question: Prolonged reliance on a strict clear fluid diet without supplementation leads to what outcome?

options.A: Delayed healing and muscle breakdown
options.B: Sudden overload of serum iron levels
options.C: Rapid increase in subcutaneous fat stores
options.D: Permanent improvement in digestive enzymes

explanation: Without adequate protein and calories, the body breaks down its own tissues to meet energy demands, delaying recovery. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h4)

question: What assessment must be performed before offering oral fluids to a post-stroke patient?

options.A: Daily fasting blood glucose levels
options.B: Swallowing capability and gag reflex
options.C: Circumference of the upper arm
options.D: Peripheral pulse and blood pressure

explanation: Checking the gag reflex and swallow safety prevents accidental aspiration of liquids into the respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h5)

question: A patient refuses hospital-provided clear broths due to personal beliefs. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Document that the patient is uncooperative with the medical plan
options.B: Consult dietary services to find culturally acceptable clear fluid alternatives
options.C: Insist that the patient drinks the broth to prevent dehydration
options.D: Immediately upgrade the patient to a regular solid food diet

explanation: Respecting patient preferences while maintaining the prescribed diet type ensures better intake and compliance. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h5)

question: What is the correct posture for a patient receiving oral fluids in bed?

options.A: Lying entirely on the left lateral side
options.B: Sitting upright at a 90-degree angle
options.C: Reclining at a 30-degree bed elevation
options.D: Flat on the back with one small pillow

explanation: An upright posture uses gravity to facilitate safe swallowing and reduces the risk of liquid aspiration. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h6)

question: Why are thickening agents sometimes added to liquids for patients with swallowing difficulties?

options.A: They turn liquid meals into solid food immediately
options.B: They increase the overall protein content of the water
options.C: They slow down fluid movement to allow better swallowing control
options.D: They mask unpleasant medication tastes in clear broths

explanation: Thicker liquids move more slowly in the mouth and throat, giving weak muscles time to protect the airway. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h6)

question: Which sign indicates that a patient is tolerating the transition from a fluid diet to soft foods?

options.A: Requesting discharge against medical advice
options.B: Complaining of severe hunger and thirst
options.C: Passing flatus and active bowel sounds
options.D: Sleeping continuously throughout the afternoon

explanation: Passing gas and hearing bowel sounds confirm that the gastrointestinal tract is regaining motility and ready for more complex foods. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h7)

question: A patient on a clear fluid diet for four days develops generalized weakness and confusion. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Infection from drinking unboiled tap water
options.B: A sudden allergic reaction to hospital water
options.C: Normal reaction to post-operative anesthesia
options.D: Electrolyte imbalance and calorie deprivation

explanation: Prolonged unsupplemented fluid diets deplete essential electrolytes and energy, manifesting as weakness and cognitive changes. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T001#GNS227_U6_T001_h7)

question: What is the primary characteristic of foods served on a soft diet?

options.A: They are served exclusively at freezing temperatures
options.B: They are easy to chew and swallow
options.C: They contain no carbohydrates or fats
options.D: They must be completely blended into liquids

explanation: Soft diets feature foods selected specifically for their tender texture requiring minimal chewing effort. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h1)

question: Why is moisture often added to foods prepared for a soft diet?

options.A: To prevent bacterial growth during storage
options.B: To make swallowing safer and easier
options.C: To extend the shelf life of the meal
options.D: To increase the overall sodium content

explanation: Adding gravies, broths, or sauces helps lubricate tender foods to assist patients with swallowing difficulties. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h1)

question: A patient recovering from which procedure is most likely to receive a soft diet?

options.A: Appendectomy closure
options.B: Cataract removal surgery
options.C: Below-knee amputation
options.D: Dental extractions

explanation: Dental procedures and oral surgeries directly impact a patient's ability to chew hard foods, necessitating a soft diet. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h2)

question: At what stage of recovery is a soft diet typically introduced after major surgery?

options.A: Immediately before the patient enters the operating theatre
options.B: Only when the patient develops a severe systemic infection
options.C: As a permanent replacement for intravenous feeding forever
options.D: During the transition from liquid diets to regular food

explanation: Soft diets serve as a safe stepping stone to test gastrointestinal tolerance before returning to regular solid foods. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h2)

question: What distinguishes a pureed diet from a mechanical soft diet?

options.A: Pureed diets require vigorous chewing from the patient
options.B: Mechanical soft foods are strictly served as cold liquids
options.C: Pureed foods are blended into a smooth pudding texture
options.D: Mechanical soft foods contain no protein or vitamins

explanation: A pureed diet requires no chewing because foods are blended entirely smooth, unlike mechanical soft diets which still contain small, tender pieces. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h3)

question: When is a mechanical soft diet preferred over a pureed diet?

options.A: When the patient can handle small, tender pieces of food
options.B: When the patient refuses to take any form of oral medication
options.C: When the doctor wants to restrict all fluid intake entirely
options.D: When the patient has complete paralysis of the swallowing muscles

explanation: Mechanical soft diets allow minced or chopped textures, which are suitable for patients who still have some chewing capability. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h3)

question: What is a major risk when a patient is placed on a textured modified diet?

options.A: Instantaneous cure of all underlying chronic illnesses
options.B: Total elimination of fluid requirements in the body
options.C: Inadequate nutritional intake and calorie reduction
options.D: Rapid and dangerous weight gain from high activity

explanation: Patients often eat less when food textures are restricted, which can lead to unintentional weight loss and nutrient deficiencies. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h4)

question: How can nurses help maintain proper nutrition for patients on a soft diet?

options.A: By including calorie-dense foods like eggs and dairy products
options.B: By removing all seasoning and flavoring from every meal
options.C: By insisting that patients eat only raw vegetables and fruits
options.D: By restricting all fluid intake during meal times completely

explanation: Adding nutrient-dense and calorie-rich options compensates for smaller portion sizes and prevents malnutrition. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h4)

question: Which fruit is generally suitable for inclusion on a soft diet without cooking?

options.A: Ripe bananas
options.B: Dry coconut chunks
options.C: Unripe guavas
options.D: Hard green mangoes

explanation: Ripe bananas have a naturally soft texture that requires minimal effort to chew and swallow safely. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h5)

question: What is the proper way to prepare vegetables for a patient on a soft diet?

options.A: Serve them raw and crisp to preserve natural vitamins
options.B: Boil or steam them until they are fork-tender
options.C: Deep-fry them in hot oil until golden brown and crunchy
options.D: Dehydrate them completely into dry vegetable chips

explanation: Cooking vegetables until they are fork-tender breaks down tough fibers, making them safe and easy to chew. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h5)

question: Which of the following food items must be avoided on a soft diet?

options.A: Popcorn and crunchy nuts
options.B: Mashed Irish potatoes
options.C: Steamed soft pumpkin
options.D: Smooth vegetable soup

explanation: Popcorn and nuts pose serious choking risks and have hard fragments that can injure sensitive tissues. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h6)

question: Why are highly spiced foods restricted for patients consuming a soft diet?

options.A: They can cause discomfort to healing oral tissues
options.B: They reduce the calorie content of the meal
options.C: They instantly cause permanent kidney failure
options.D: They make the food too soft to chew properly

explanation: Spices and acids irritate raw, healing surfaces in the mouth and gastrointestinal tract following surgery or illness. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h6)

question: What is a key sign of swallowing difficulty during meal observation?

options.A: Coughing or choking while eating
options.B: Finishing the meal in record time
options.C: Smiling happily while chewing food
options.D: Asking for an extra cup of water

explanation: Coughing or choking during meals indicates that food or liquid may be entering the airway, signaling potential dysphagia. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h7)

question: Why do nurses routinely monitor the body weight of patients on modified diets?

options.A: To determine the correct dosage of intravenous antibiotics
options.B: To detect early signs of inadequate nutritional intake
options.C: To calculate the exact daily water loss through sweat
options.D: To ensure the patient is exercising enough in bed

explanation: Weight tracking helps identify whether the patient is consuming enough calories and nutrients despite texture restrictions. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h7)

question: What should patient education include before discharge on a soft diet?

options.A: Guidelines on how to avoid all physical activity forever
options.B: Methods to perform minor surgical operations at home
options.C: Instructions on food preparation and texture identification
options.D: A strict ban on drinking any liquids for life

explanation: Caregivers and patients need practical knowledge of safe food preparation to continue proper nutrition at home. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h8)

question: How should a patient approach the return to a regular diet?

options.A: By stopping all fluid intake immediately upon starting solids
options.B: By ignoring symptoms of stomach pain and continuing to eat
options.C: By reintroducing firmer foods gradually and watching for issues
options.D: By eating a large plate of hard nuts on the very first day

explanation: A slow and cautious reintroduction helps test digestive tolerance and prevents injury to healing tissues. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h8)

question: What is the general percentage range of daily calories suggested by standard protein guidelines?

options.A: 40 to 60 percent
options.B: 70 to 85 percent
options.C: 10 to 35 percent
options.D: 5 to 10 percent

explanation: Standard dietary guidelines recommend that protein make up between 10 and 35 percent of an adult's total daily caloric intake. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h1)

question: Why do modern clinical nurses encounter high protein diets more frequently than in the past?

options.A: Hospitals banned carbohydrates entirely from clinical meal trays
options.B: Patients use them widely for weight loss and muscle preservation
options.C: Standard dietary guidelines now demand excessive protein intake
options.D: Government mandates require all citizens to consume extra meat

explanation: Widespread public interest in weight management and fitness has driven patients to adopt high protein regimens independently. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h1)

question: Which specific plasma protein plays the primary role in maintaining oncotic pressure and fluid balance?

options.A: Keratin
options.B: Hemoglobin
options.C: Albumin
options.D: Fibrinogen

explanation: Albumin is the major plasma protein responsible for maintaining intravascular oncotic pressure and keeping fluid inside blood vessels. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h2)

question: A patient with a severe protein deficiency is most at risk for developing which clinical sign?

options.A: Excessive blood clotting speed
options.B: Rapid overproduction of insulin
options.C: Generalized peripheral edema
options.D: Hypertension from thickened blood

explanation: Low blood protein levels drop oncotic pressure, allowing fluid to leak out of capillaries into surrounding tissues to cause edema. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h2)

question: What metabolic state characterizes patients with severe burns or major physical trauma?

options.A: Excessive carbohydrate retention
options.B: Positive lipid storage
options.C: Negative nitrogen balance
options.D: Complete metabolic halt

explanation: Severe physical trauma triggers rapid tissue breakdown, causing the body to excrete more nitrogen than it takes in. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h3)

question: Why is a high protein diet specifically ordered for a patient with deep pressure ulcers?

options.A: Proteins completely replace the need for sterile wound dressings
options.B: Extra protein acts as a mild topical antiseptic over the ulcer bed
options.C: High protein intake stops bacterial colonization in chronic skin wounds
options.D: Amino acids are required to synthesize new granulation tissue and heal wounds

explanation: Wound healing demands a high supply of building blocks for cell division and collagen synthesis, which extra dietary protein provides. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h3)

question: What defines a complete dietary protein source?

options.A: It requires no digestion in the stomach
options.B: It comes exclusively from plant-based foods
options.C: It has zero calories and zero fat content
options.D: It contains all nine essential amino acids

explanation: A complete protein supplies every single one of the essential amino acids that the human body cannot manufacture independently. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h4)

question: How can a patient following a strict plant-based diet ensure adequate essential amino acid intake?

options.A: Avoiding all forms of soy and legume products entirely
options.B: Consuming a variety of complementary plant proteins over the course of the day
options.C: Taking high-dose iron supplements with every single meal
options.D: Eating only raw green vegetables and drinking distilled water

explanation: Since individual plant foods may lack certain amino acids, mixing different plant sources ensures the body receives all necessary building blocks. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h4)

question: What is the standard baseline RDA for protein in a healthy sedentary adult?

options.A: 2.5 grams per kilogram
options.B: 5.0 grams per kilogram
options.C: 0.8 grams per kilogram
options.D: 0.2 grams per kilogram

explanation: The baseline recommended dietary allowance for healthy, non-athletic adults sits at 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight daily. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h5)

question: Which lab marker should a nurse interpret cautiously when assessing nutrition in an acutely inflamed patient?

options.A: Blood glucose
options.B: Serum sodium
options.C: Serum albumin
options.D: Platelet count

explanation: Albumin acts as a negative acute-phase reactant, meaning its blood levels drop during active inflammation regardless of true nutritional status. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h5)

question: What is a practical strategy for a nurse to help a patient who struggles to finish large high-protein meals?

options.A: Provide smaller, frequent protein-rich snacks throughout the day
options.B: Remove all solid food and rely entirely on water intake
options.C: Scold the patient for showing poor compliance with the diet
options.D: Force the patient to finish every bite before leaving the room

explanation: Dividing high-protein foods into smaller, frequent portions prevents the patient from feeling overwhelmed by large meals and improves total daily intake. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h6)

question: A patient on a high protein regimen begins refusing water because they feel full. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Explain that extra protein intake requires increased fluid to protect kidney function
options.B: Document that the patient refuses to cooperate with basic ward routines
options.C: Withhold all further protein supplements until fluid intake normalizes completely
options.D: Replace all drinking water with thick sugary juices to boost calories

explanation: Higher protein loads increase metabolic waste products that require adequate renal clearance, making proper hydration essential. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h6)

question: Which organ system faces the primary workload increase when processing a chronic excess of dietary protein?

options.A: Neurological system
options.B: Integumentary system
options.C: Renal system
options.D: Respiratory system

explanation: The kidneys filter and excrete nitrogenous waste products resulting from protein metabolism, bearing the brunt of excess intake. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h7)

question: Why might a patient following an unmonitored high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet develop frequent constipation?

options.A: Severe restriction of carbohydrate-rich foods typically reduces daily dietary fiber intake
options.B: High protein diets completely shut down large bowel motility permanently
options.C: Proteins absorb all available water in the stomach before digestion begins
options.D: Excess protein coats the intestinal walls and stops normal peristalsis

explanation: Cutting out grains, fruits, and starchy vegetables often eliminates the primary sources of dietary fiber needed for regular bowel movements. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T003#GNS227_U6_T003_h7)

question: What is the primary waste product formed from dietary protein breakdown that accumulates during renal failure?

options.A: Bicarbonate
options.B: Glucose
options.C: Urea
options.D: Lactic acid

explanation: Protein metabolism produces nitrogenous waste, primarily urea, which the failing kidneys cannot efficiently clear from the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h1)

question: Why is a low protein diet often given to patients with severe liver disease?

options.A: To stimulate rapid regeneration of damaged liver cells
options.B: To prevent dangerous ammonia buildup in the brain
options.C: To stop the sudden accumulation of blood urea nitrogen
options.D: To lower systemic blood pressure within the portal vein

explanation: Undigested proteins and amino acids break down into ammonia in the gut, which a failing liver cannot process into urea safely. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h1)

question: At which stages of chronic kidney disease is protein restriction typically recommended?

options.A: Stage one exclusively
options.B: One and two only
options.C: Three through five
options.D: All stages equally

explanation: Moderate to advanced chronic kidney disease stages 3 to 5 benefit most from reducing protein intake to slow nephron destruction. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h2)

question: A patient with liver cirrhosis becomes confused and sleepy. Restricting dietary protein helps mainly by:

options.A: Preventing severe muscle wasting in the lower limbs
options.B: Decreasing bowel production of neurotoxic ammonia
options.C: Stopping sudden fluid shifts into the peritoneal cavity
options.D: Correcting low serum albumin levels in the blood

explanation: Limiting protein substrate for gut bacteria lowers ammonia levels, reducing cerebral toxicity in hepatic encephalopathy. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h2)

question: What is the usual daily protein allowance for a moderate low-protein diet in chronic kidney disease?

options.A: Two point zero grams per kilogram daily
options.B: Zero point one grams per kilogram daily
options.C: Zero point six grams per kilogram daily
options.D: One point five grams per kilogram daily

explanation: Standard moderate protein restriction targets approximately 0.6g/kg/day to reduce renal load while avoiding rapid wasting. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h3)

question: When patients are placed on a very strict low-protein diet, what supplements are usually required?

options.A: Pure mineral electrolyte mixtures
options.B: Concentrated liquid glucose solutions
options.C: Essential amino acids or ketoanalogues
options.D: High doses of water-soluble vitamins

explanation: Strict restriction prevents adequate intake of essential building blocks, necessitating supplements to prevent severe tissue breakdown. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h3)

question: Which blood test is commonly checked to assess a patient's protein status, even though inflammation can alter its levels?

options.A: Serum sodium
options.B: Serum albumin
options.C: Serum calcium
options.D: Serum glucose

explanation: Serum albumin helps evaluate visceral protein stores, though inflammation can cause levels to drop independently of diet. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h4)

question: Why do nurses measure the mid-arm muscle circumference during nutritional assessments?

options.A: To check for local tissue edema from low protein
options.B: To check for unintended loss of skeletal muscle mass
options.C: To detect peripheral nerve damage from uremia
options.D: To watch for acute fluid overload in the extremities

explanation: Anthropometric checks track somatic protein stores and lean body mass changes over time during dietary restrictions. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h4)

question: What are proteins called when they contain all the essential amino acids the body needs?

options.A: Incomplete plant proteins
options.B: Low biological value proteins
options.C: High biological value proteins
options.D: Non-essential amino acids

explanation: High biological value proteins supply all indispensable amino acids required by the human body efficiently. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h5)

question: Why is it important to ensure a high intake of carbohydrates and fats for patients on a protein-restricted diet?

options.A: To enhance the absorption of dietary minerals in the gut
options.B: To provide adequate calories and prevent muscle breakdown
options.C: To directly bind excess urea and clear it through stool
options.D: To stimulate the pancreas to produce digestive enzymes

explanation: Sufficient non-protein calories ensure the body uses dietary energy sources rather than breaking down its own muscle. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h5)

question: What is a major risk of a long-term, unmonitored low-protein diet?

options.A: Elevated serum iron levels
options.B: Rapid muscle hypertrophy
options.C: Excessive bone mineralization
options.D: Protein-energy wasting

explanation: Inadequate protein and calorie intake leads to protein-energy wasting, increasing morbidity and mortality in chronic illness. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h6)

question: Why do vitamin and mineral deficiencies often develop when a patient is on a low-protein diet?

options.A: Carbohydrates actively bind and destroy dietary iron
options.B: The liver stops absorbing trace elements from the diet
options.C: Kidneys excrete all vitamins rapidly in low protein states
options.D: Common protein foods also supply essential vitamins and minerals

explanation: Common protein sources like meat and dairy are primary dietary suppliers of iron, zinc, and B vitamins. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h6)

question: What is a key nursing duty when caring for a patient on a low-protein diet?

options.A: Preparing all daily meals in the hospital kitchen
options.B: Administering intravenous amino acid infusions daily
options.C: Monitoring laboratory results and nutritional status
options.D: Prescribing the exact daily gram limit of protein

explanation: Nurses track biochemical markers and physical signs of malnutrition to evaluate tolerance of the dietary restriction. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h7)

question: Which dietary tip should a nurse give to a patient who is on a low-protein diet?

options.A: Using calorie-dense, low-protein foods to maintain energy
options.B: Replacing high biological value proteins with plant sources
options.C: Increasing water intake to five liters with every meal
options.D: Completely eliminating all forms of fats and carbohydrates

explanation: Adding healthy fats and simple sugars prevents weight loss and energy deficits while keeping protein intake restricted. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T004#GNS227_U6_T004_h7)

question: What is the typical upper limit of daily fat intake in a standard low fat diet expressed as a percentage of total calories?

options.A: More than 90 percent
options.B: Exactly 50 percent
options.C: Less than 30 percent
options.D: Around 75 percent

explanation: Therapeutic low fat diets generally restrict total fat intake to under 30% of daily energy needs. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h1)

question: A patient believes a low fat diet means eating zero grams of fat daily. How should the nurse correct this?

options.A: Confirm that all fats must be completely removed to see any clinical benefit
options.B: Explain that the diet aims for moderation and selective reduction rather than absolute elimination
options.C: Suggest stopping the diet entirely until a dietitian is available to rewrite it
options.D: Advise the patient to replace all fats with simple sugars for energy

explanation: Essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins are still required, so the diet focuses on reducing quantity and improving quality rather than zero intake. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h1)

question: Which group of vitamins depends heavily on dietary fats for proper absorption in the gut?

options.A: B-complex vitamins
options.B: Ascorbic acid vitamins
options.C: Water-soluble vitamins
options.D: Fat-soluble vitamins

explanation: Vitamins A, D, E, and K require dietary fat and bile salts to be properly absorbed through the intestinal mucosa. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h2)

question: A patient with acute cholecystitis experiences severe abdominal pain after eating fatty meals. What is the physiological reason for this?

options.A: Fats stimulate cholecystokinin release which causes painful gallbladder contractions
options.B: Fats ferment quickly in the stomach and create excessive gas pressure
options.C: Fats neutralize stomach acid and irritate the lining of the small intestine
options.D: Lipids crystallize rapidly inside the pancreatic duct and block insulin output

explanation: Dietary fats trigger the hormone cholecystokinin, causing the inflamed gallbladder to contract against blockages or stones, resulting in pain. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h2)

question: Which type of dietary fat is artificially produced through hydrogenation and poses a high cardiovascular risk?

options.A: Saturated fats
options.B: Polyunsaturated fats
options.C: Trans fats
options.D: Monounsaturated fats

explanation: Trans fats are created by adding hydrogen to liquid vegetable oils to make them more solid, which increases harmful cholesterol levels. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h3)

question: Why are monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats generally preferred over saturated fats in a healthy meal plan?

options.A: They do not require any digestive enzymes to break down
options.B: They contain zero calories compared to saturated fats
options.C: They completely prevent the development of gallstones
options.D: They help maintain or improve favorable blood cholesterol profiles

explanation: Unsaturated fats help lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and protect heart health compared to saturated and trans fats. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h3)

question: What is the primary rationale for prescribing a low fat diet to a patient with acute pancreatitis?

options.A: To reduce pancreatic enzyme secretion and prevent auto-digestion
options.B: To increase the production of alkaline bile in the liver
options.C: To stimulate rapid insulin release from the islets of Langerhans
options.D: To speed up gastric emptying time in the stomach

explanation: Lowering dietary fat decreases the stimulation of the pancreas, allowing the inflamed organ time to rest and heal. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h4)

question: A patient with chronic malabsorption is passing pale, bulky, and foul-smelling stools. What is this clinical finding called?

options.A: Glycosuria
options.B: Steatorrhea
options.C: Hematuria
options.D: Melena

explanation: Steatorrhea is the presence of excess fat in feces, which occurs when dietary fats are poorly digested or absorbed in the gut. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h4)

question: Which food item is appropriate for inclusion in a strict low fat meal plan?

options.A: Skinless chicken breast
options.B: Deep-fried plantain chips
options.C: Full-fat cheddar cheese
options.D: Rich creamy alfredo sauce

explanation: Skinless poultry is a lean protein source that contains minimal saturated fat compared to dairy, red meat, or fried items. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T005#GNS227_U6_T005_h5)

question: Why are commercially processed baked goods discouraged on a low fat diet?

options.A: They frequently contain hidden fats and hydrogenated oils
options.B: They lack any carbohydrate content whatsoever
